content: Hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection is a significant cause of illness and death in the United States. Over half of individuals who contract HCV will develop chronic infection. Direct-acting antiviral (DAA) treatments have revolutionized HCV management, offering a virologic cure for most patients within 8 to 12 weeks of all-oral medication regimens. These treatments are highly effective, with approximately 90% of HCV-infected individuals achieving sustained virologic response (SVR), which is indicative of a cure. However, DAAs are not yet approved for use during pregnancy, and safety data in this population remain limited. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has updated its recommendations for HCV testing in the United States. These include universal hepatitis C screening at least once in a lifetime for all adults aged 18 years and older, except in settings where the prevalence of HCV infection is less than 0.1%. Additionally, the CDC now recommends hepatitis C screening for all pregnant women during each pregnancy, except in low-prevalence settings. These updates aim to address the increasing incidence of HCV infections, particularly among reproductive-aged adults and women with live births. HCV is the most commonly reported bloodborne infection in the United States, with an estimated 2.4 million individuals living with the virus between 2013 and 2016. Injection drug use remains the primary risk factor for HCV transmission, and national surveillance data have shown a steady increase in acute HCV cases from 2009 to 2017, particularly among individuals aged 20 to 39 years. The rise in new infections among reproductive-aged adults has also led to a near doubling of HCV infection rates among women with live births between 2009 and 2014. HCV is a small, single-stranded RNA virus belonging to the Flavivirus family, characterized by significant genetic heterogeneity. Seven distinct genotypes have been identified, with genotype 1 being the most prevalent in the United States and globally. High mutation rates in the HCV RNA genome contribute to the virus's ability to evade the immune system. Prior infection with HCV does not confer immunity against subsequent infections, even with the same or different genotypes. HCV can be detected in saliva, semen, breast milk, and other body fluids, but these are not considered efficient vehicles for transmission. Persons at risk for HCV infection include those who inject drugs, individuals undergoing invasive medical procedures without proper infection control, and healthcare workers exposed to needlestick injuries. Perinatal transmission is a growing concern due to the increasing incidence of HCV among women of childbearing age. Acute HCV infection is often asymptomatic or presents with mild symptoms similar to other types of viral hepatitis. Jaundice occurs in 20-30% of cases, while nonspecific symptoms such as anorexia, malaise, or abdominal pain are reported in 10-20% of cases. Fulminant hepatic failure following acute HCV infection is rare. Chronic HCV infection develops when the virus evades the host immune response, leading to a slow and insidious progression of liver disease over decades. Approximately 5-25% of individuals with chronic HCV will develop cirrhosis within 10-20 years, with an annual risk of 1-4% for hepatocellular carcinoma among those with cirrhosis. Extrahepatic manifestations of chronic HCV infection include membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis, essential mixed cryoglobulinemia, porphyria cutanea tarda, and lymphoma. Predictors of spontaneous clearance of HCV include jaundice, elevated alanine aminotransferase (ALT) levels, female sex, younger age, and certain genetic polymorphisms near the IL28B gene. The CDC's updated recommendations emphasize the importance of universal HCV screening to improve diagnosis and linkage to care. Testing during pregnancy provides an opportunity to identify infected mothers and infants, enabling timely interventions to reduce perinatal transmission risks. While DAAs are not yet approved for use in pregnancy, testing pregnant women for HCV remains beneficial for both maternal and infant health. The postpartum period offers a unique opportunity to transition women diagnosed with HCV during pregnancy to treatment with DAAs, reducing the risk of transmission in subsequent pregnancies. The CDC's recommendations are based on comprehensive systematic reviews of the literature, which examined the prevalence of HCV infection and the health benefits and harms associated with one-time hepatitis C screening. These reviews were conducted in two stages: one focused on all adults and the other on pregnant women. The evidence supports the implementation of universal HCV screening strategies to address the ongoing public health burden of hepatitis C in the United States.
